title: Winter and Harvest
premise: Mirabel Blackwood hosts a late-night call-in show in the dying town of Harrow Creek, where listeners begin phoning in — people who died the week before, asking her to pass messages to the living. When her own sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, Mirabel learns the dead are being funneled through an old well on her family's land, and that in 1974 her grandmother stole something from it: a name, and with it, a life. As the town's found family of insomniacs, skeptics, and mourners closes ranks around her, Mirabel must choose between protecting the woman who raised her and telling the truth that will free the trapped dead. She returns the stolen name to the well before it refills at the winter solstice, losing her grandmother's memory of her but gaining a family bound by truth instead of silence.
about_author: Quentin Ishikawa is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent six years answering calls from strangers at 3 a.m. and swears half of them were already gone. They write horror about small towns, old debts, and the voices we pretend not to hear.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. During her regular broadcast, a caller asks after his wife — then his obituary airs on the news mid-call. Mirabel assumes a prank, but her hands shake through the rest of the shift. Emotional beat: denial established as armor.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Reviewing her sleep-recording app for insomnia, she hears herself ask questions in her sleep — and something else answer in a voice like wet gravel. It says her grandmother's maiden name. Emotional beat: dread creeping past skepticism.

chapters.title: Messages, Please
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Mirabel and Ruthie, a diner widow. More dead callers phone in, each with a message for someone living. Ruthie receives one from her son; Mirabel records every call, telling herself it's research. Emotional beat: grief as contagion.

chapters.title: Harrow Creek Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She digs into town archives for the 1974 incident her grandmother never discusses. Records are missing; the librarian warns her off with genuine fear. Emotional beat: the cost of asking questions in a town built on not-asking.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Grandmother Edith's POV, 1974 flashbacks braided with present. Young Edith and her sister Lorna visit the well behind the Blackwood house; only one girl comes home whole. Present-day Edith burns a box of letters. Emotional beat: love curdling into concealment.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The second voice grows clearer: the well 'refills' each solstice, taking new sleepers to replace what was taken. Her neighbor's child begins sleep-talking in a dead man's voice. Emotional beat: stakes become communal, not personal.

chapters.title: Found Family, 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The night-shift regulars — Ruthie, dispatcher Cole, teen insomniac Dev — form an impromptu vigil crew around Mirabel's broadcasts, cross-checking the dead callers' claims. Emotional beat: warmth kindling inside horror.

chapters.title: Lorna
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The second voice identifies itself: Lorna, Edith's sister, drowned in 1974 and never buried properly because there was no body. She wants her name back. Emotional beat: the skeptic meets her first undeniable ghost.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Cole's POV. Cole discovers Edith has been quietly paying the well's toll for fifty years — small disappearances, kept small. He must decide whether to tell Mirabel. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made literal.

chapters.title: The Toll Book
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The teens find Edith's ledger hidden in the storm cellar: names, dates, payments. Every entry is in Edith's hand except one — Lorna's, crossed out. Emotional beat: betrayal arriving as paperwork.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel confronts Edith with the ledger. Edith admits she took Lorna's name in 1974 to save her own daughter — Mirabel's mother — from the well. Emotional beat: love against duty, both sides bleeding.

chapters.title: Static Wedding
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. The dead callers begin speaking over one another, their messages tangling into demands. Ruthie's son's message turns out to be a lure from the well itself. Emotional beat: grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Sleepers
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Solstice approaches; sleepers across town stop waking. Dev nearly doesn't. The found family moves into the Blackwood house together, barricading nights with coffee, radios, and prayer. Emotional beat: chosen family holding the line.

chapters.title: What the Well Wants
chapters.summary: Lorna's POV (through recordings). Lorna explains the bargain: return the name before the solstice, or the well takes a life to balance the ledger — and it prefers children now. Emotional beat: mercy with teeth.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Broadcast
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel puts Edith's confession on air, breaking the town's fifty-year silence. Callers flood in — living and dead — some grateful, some furious. Emotional beat: truth as detonation.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: Cole's POV. The solstice eve. Power fails, roads ice over, and the well's pull reaches through every radio in town. The group fortifies the house as the temperature drops impossibly. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The well takes Dev in his sleep. Mirabel hears him calling from inside it. With hours left, she races Edith to the wellhead through the blizzard while Cole keeps Dev's body breathing. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the well, Mirabel speaks Lorna's name back into the dark, offering the ledger page as proof of restitution. The well demands a keeper instead of a victim. Emotional beat: climax — the price renegotiated.

chapters.title: The Keeper
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith volunteers herself, fifty years of guilt finally spent. She steps to the wellhead as its keeper, trading memory of Mirabel for the town's sleepers. Emotional beat: sacrifice as atonement, love outlasting memory.

chapters.title: Morning After the Longest Night
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Dawn. Sleepers wake, including Dev. The dead callers go quiet, their messages delivered or released. Edith looks at Mirabel with polite stranger's eyes. Emotional beat: victory shadowed by loss.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel rebuilds the show around honest talk — grief, memory, the things towns bury. She reads Lorna's restored name into the record. Emotional beat: turning witness into vocation.

chapters.title: Winter and Harvest
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, epilogue. Spring planting beside the sealed well; Edith tends the garden without knowing why she chose it. Mirabel finds a note in Edith's handwriting she doesn't remember writing: 'Keep them fed, keep them loved.' Emotional beat: found family enduring beyond memory.
